summary: A wooden lighthouse built in 1858 after the first one landed on the wrong island, replaced in 1897 by an iron tower on a sandy spit in the Apostle Islands.

structures.note: First lighthouse with a 35-foot wooden tower; tower and lantern removed in the 1896-97 rebuild into a duplex; abandoned about 1940
Height disputed: 60 ft, 65 ft 3 in or 67 ft

access.note: Not open to the public and not served by scheduled tour boats; Apostle Islands National Lakeshore; light maintained by the Coast Guard. Distant views from Madeline Island and State Highway 13.

facts.agency: National Park Service (island); U.S. Coast Guard (aid to navigation)

events.note: Lighthouse Board secured a 152-acre reservation on Long Island on 28 April 1853
First La Pointe lighthouse completed on Long Island (HAER card says built 1856)
Stone pier foundation placed beneath the first lighthouse (Lighthousefriends); the NPS inventory says crushed stone was placed around it in 1869
Steam fog signal begun October 1890, completed January 1891, three-fourths of a mile east of the light; first blew 3 January 1891
Congress appropriated $10,000 on 2 March 1895 for moving and rebuilding the main La Pointe light and a Chequamegon Point light
Skeletal iron tower completed and lit 11 October 1897; old lighthouse raised on a brick basement and made a duplex
Steam whistle replaced by an air diaphone
Both towers converted to electric lamps on 3 August 1937
Triplex keepers' quarters built (PWA project); full occupancy 1940
Coast Guard took over the lighthouses
Coast Guard installed automated lights in both towers; keepers left
Listed 4 August 1983 in a multiple-property nomination of Coast Guard lighthouses on the Great Lakes
Long Island added to Apostle Islands National Lakeshore (the island itself is not open as a visitor site)
Fog signal building demolished by the Coast Guard (after 1986 per the NPS inventory)

to build cribs to protect his garden from the eroding shoreline. Other keepers did not have Sexton’s green
thumb. Lighthouse keeper, Ben Hudak, who served at LaPointe in the 1930s, recalled in an oral history
interview that they could not have a garden or plant anything on the island, mostly because of the sandy
soil. He noted that wild blueberries and cranberries grew there. The light keepers left other marks on the
area. In the July 1897 log the keeper reported he chopped the timber down across the point to get the wind
to drive the flies away “...for they are very bad”.
The dynamic shoreline caused problems for the station. In 1902 the dock was repaired and extended and
the water supply intake for the fog signal was rebuilt to reduce silt build up. In 1911, work crews installed
three 32 foot long log cribs filled with crushed stone along the northwest side of the point to protect the
Chequamegon tower footings.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The first lighthouse on Long Island was completed and lit in 1858 (HAER card: 1856); the present skeletal tower was built 1896-97 and first lit 11 October 1897, so the record's 1896 'built/first_lit/deactivated' entries for 'Tower 2' mark the start of construction, not a lighting.

The Light-House Board bought a '60-foot skeleton metal tower' (FY1897); the HAER card measures 65 ft 3 in to the top of the ventilator ball; the NPS inventory says sixty-seven foot; USLHS gives 60.75 ft base to lantern centre.

notes_for_editor: No newspaper hits were found through newspapers.py (searched Sexton, La Pointe/Long Island/Bayfield lighthouse); the Sexton log entries and the 1919 Bayfield County Press article are quoted second-hand from Lighthousefriends (cite 3) and are footnoted as such. NPS inventory (cite 1) is a two-column PDF; quotes were taken from single column segments. Disagreements stated in the text: 1858 vs 1856 first lighthouse; foundation work 1864/1868 (Lighthousefriends) vs 1869 (NPS); 1897 appropriation date (4 June in the Board report, 14 July in NPS); tower height (60 ft, 65 ft 3 in, 67 ft); which tower received the Le Paute/old lens (HAER and NPS say the old lens went to Chequamegon Point; NPS also says a Le Paute fourth-order lens shone from La Pointe; Lighthousefriends says Henry-Lepaute at La Pointe); automation 1964 vs 1965 (unmanned) vs 1968 (NPS summary); Hudak head keeper 1946 (USLHS) vs 1948 (Lighthouse Digest, Lighthousefriends); Hudak at La Pointe from 1928 (USLHS) vs February 1930 (Lighthouse Digest); old house abandoned about 1940 (NPS) vs 1938 (Lighthouse Digest). The fog-signal hours figure labelled fiscal 1895 comes from the volume the corpus labels 1895/1896 whose text has no title page; it is dated by its contents (act of 2 March 1895 'negotiations in progress') and the page is not determined; the fiscal 1897 entries are from the volume with the FY1896 title page and the 1897 sections, page not determined (corpus has no page index for it). Orasmus Cole is called a senator by the NPS inventory and a congressman by Lighthousefriends; the story gives no title. Ed Sexton being Joseph Sexton's son rests on Lighthousefriends alone. The Chequamegon Point Light (us-wi-chequamegon-point) has its own station record. A 'Mary Haloran' appears as first assistant 1857-58 in the archive roster; the relationship to John Haloran is not stated by any source and the story does not assume one. Hudak's quote of 1959 is as reported by Lighthouse Digest from the Minneapolis Star. No photos added.
